# Systems and applications
## Overview
This family encompasses the deployment, integration, and hardware acceleration of volume rendering techniques in real-world scenarios. It addresses the gap between theoretical rendering algorithms and practical implementation constraints, such as computational intensity, display hardware limitations, and user interaction requirements. It is distinguished from [Image-order rendering](16-image-order-rendering.md) and [Object-order rendering](22-object-order-rendering.md) by its focus on the system-level architecture (e.g., GPU pipelines, web browsers, physical displays) rather than the specific sampling or shading strategies used per pixel or voxel.

## Shared principles
The articles in this family share the goal of mapping abstract volumetric data $I(x,y,z)$ to a perceptible output through specific system constraints. Common mechanisms include:
1.  **Hardware Acceleration Mapping**: Offloading computationally intensive tasks (ray casting, splatting, sorting) to parallel execution units (GPUs, multi-core CPUs) to achieve real-time or near-real-time performance [S1, unofficial].
2.  **Data Structure Optimization**: Storing volumetric data in formats optimized for the target hardware, such as 3D/4D textures for coalesced memory access on GPUs or sparse structures (e.g., OpenVDB) for memory efficiency [S1, unofficial].
3.  **Depth Management**: Handling the ordering of contributions for alpha-blended rendering, often requiring GPU-based sorting algorithms (radix sort, linked lists) to ensure correct compositing [S1, unofficial].
4.  **Physical-to-Digital Mapping**: In the case of volumetric displays, transforming 3D voxel coordinates into 2D control signals (pixel buffers, SLM patterns) synchronized with mechanical or optical processes to create a physical 3D light field [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Voxel engines and games](47-voxel-engines-and-games.md)
Focuses on integrating volume rendering into game engines, often using voxel-based representations for dynamic environments.

### [Film and production rendering](48-film-and-production-rendering.md)
Covers high-fidelity rendering pipelines for visual effects, particularly for clouds, fire, and smoke, often using VDB data structures.

### [Scientific and medical visualization](49-scientific-and-medical-visualization.md)
Applies volume rendering to analyze and interpret complex datasets from scientific simulations or medical imaging (CT, MRI).

### [GPU, web and parallel renderers](50-gpu-web-and-parallel-renderers.md)
This family encompasses rendering systems that offload volume rendering computations to parallel hardware (GPUs, multi-core CPUs) or execute entirely within web browsers using WebGL/WebGPU. It addresses the computational intensity of volume rendering by leveraging massive parallelism for tasks like ray casting, splatting, and data sorting. It is distinguished from [Voxel engines and games](47-voxel-engines-and-games.md) by its focus on general-purpose visualization rather than game engine integration, and from [Film and production rendering](48-film-and-production-rendering.md) by its emphasis on real-time or near-real-time interactivity and web compatibility.

### [Volumetric displays and holography](51-volumetric-displays-and-holography.md)
This family covers hardware systems and computational methods that render volumetric data directly into physical space, creating images that occupy a 3D volume visible from multiple viewpoints without headgear. It differs from standard rasterization or ray marching by projecting light into a physical medium (air, glass, or light fields) rather than onto a 2D sensor or screen. It is distinct from [Voxel engines and games](47-voxel-engines-and-games.md) which simulate volume appearance on 2D displays, and from [Scientific and medical visualization](49-scientific-and-medical-visualization.md) which typically uses 2D slice views or volume rendering on monitors.

## Background
Volume rendering has evolved from offline scientific visualization tools to real-time interactive systems and specialized hardware displays. The integration of GPUs has been a major driver, enabling complex shading and large datasets to be rendered interactively. More recently, web-based technologies (WebGL/WebGPU) have democratized access to volume visualization, while volumetric displays offer a new paradigm for 3D data presentation without stereoscopic headgear.
